title: How Moral Beliefs Influence Collective Violence. Evidence From Lynching in Mexico

selected_claim.evidence_location: Figure 5 and the Findings section, “Group-Oriented Moral Beliefs”; full regression tables A5.13–A5.14. The demanding specification is described in “Analysis Procedures.”
selected_claim.evidence_summary: In the observational analysis, higher group-oriented moral beliefs are positively associated with the paper’s measures of support for lynching. The association appears across the support items, although some estimates are not distinguishable from zero. The paper reports that the largest coefficient is for willingness to participate in the future: a one-point increase in group-oriented beliefs is associated with a 0.27-point increase on that outcome. These are adjusted observational associations, not randomized effects.
selected_claim.x: Group-oriented moral beliefs, measured as the respondent’s MFQ binding-foundations score (loyalty, authority, and purity) minus their individualizing-foundations score (harm avoidance and fairness).
selected_claim.y: Respondent favorability toward lynching, measured using responses to the vignette-based lynching-support questions, including agreement with lynching and willingness to participate.
selected_claim.target_population: Adult residents of Mexico City represented by the February 2022 face-to-face survey (N = 2,183).
selected_claim.adjustment_description: The demanding OLS specification adjusts for demographic and individual-level covariates, street-block characteristics, and colonia fixed effects, with robust standard errors clustered by colonia.
covariates: Variable to correct for systematic response bias in the questionnaire

selected_claim.mixed_methods_boundary: The paper also includes a randomized moral-priming experiment, but that experiment estimates the effect of the priming treatment on lynching attitudes and emotions. evidence_summary: The paper estimates the association between respondents’ relative endorsement of group-oriented (binding) moral foundations and favorability toward lynching in a February 2022 face-to-face survey of 2,183 adult Mexico City residents. Its demanding OLS specification adjusts for demographic and individual-level covariates and street-block characteristics, includes colonia fixed effects, and uses robust standard errors clustered by colonia. The provided claim describes an observational adjusted estimate; no numerical effect estimate or additional causal-identification details were supplied.
x_definition: Respondent endorsement of binding/group-oriented moral foundations—loyalty, authority, and purity/sanctity—relative to individualizing foundations such as harm avoidance and fairness, understood as a general moral-foundations orientation across measures and contexts.
y_definition: Respondent normative favorability, agreement, or support for lynching and related vigilantism/extralegal collective punishment, including willingness to participate, across measures and scenarios.

confounders.reason: Colonia fixed effects (c12) absorb variation in communication environments shared by respondents within a colonia during the survey period. This is design-based adjustment, not a direct control or an individual-level proxy; it does not absorb differences in respondents’ own media, message, or cue exposure within the same colonia.

graph_results.rereview_after_decisions: The updated distance-one graph was recomputed after review.

limitations: The snapshot contains focal variables for both constructs, including a lynching favorability measure, but the evidence queue links only available snapshot studies; it may not represent all relevant literature.

The claim supplied provides no numerical estimate, confidence interval, or further identification strategy beyond adjusted OLS; causal interpretation remains subject to observational confounding and measurement limitations.
The paper’s sample is adult residents represented by a Mexico City survey; generalization beyond that population, setting, and survey period is uncertain.
The outcome group is compact and includes lynching and vigilantism measures; evidence on general punitive attitudes is not equivalent to evidence on approval of extralegal collective violence.
The exposure is a relative binding-minus-individualizing score, while the broader group also contains measures of binding or group-oriented moral foundations that may not use that exact contrast.
